title: Ignition delay against 1000/T: does the model follow the experiments across temperature?
summary: The standard plot for autoignition data. A logarithmic delay axis against 1000/T turns an Arrhenius-like temperature dependence into a straight line, so slope, curvature and model-versus-experiment agreement can all be judged by eye.

media.alt: Semi-log plot of ignition delay against 1000/T, three equivalence ratios, markers for synthetic experiments and straight lines for a model.
media.caption: Reference render of class F9.1 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Does it match autoignition data?
read_the_figure.axes: x: 1000/T in 1/K (hot on the left). y: ignition delay in seconds on a log scale.
look_at: Are markers (experiment) scattered evenly on both sides of their line (model), over the whole x range?
Are the lines straight, or do they bend? A bend marks a change of controlling chemistry.
How far apart are the series vertically? Equal gaps on a log axis are equal ratios.
Are the slopes about equal across series? Parallel series share an apparent activation energy.
read_the_figure.proves: A model that threads the markers over the whole temperature range reproduces the temperature dependence, not just one point. It does not by itself prove the mechanism is right.
if_wrong: Systematic drift of markers away from the line at one end: the effective activation energy is off in that range.
Markers on a curve while the model is a line: the model lacks the regime change.
Pressure or composition missing from the legend: the plot cannot be compared with anything.
must_check: pressure and equivalence ratio stated for each series

terms.meaning: Time from the start of a constant-condition experiment to ignition, defined by a temperature rise or a radical peak. State the definition when you publish.
Reciprocal temperature scaled by a thousand so that the tick labels are of order one.
The slope of ln tau against 1/T times the gas constant: a summary of a many-step process.
Fuel-to-oxidiser ratio relative to stoichiometric: 1 is exact, below 1 lean, above 1 rich.
One axis logarithmic, one linear. Here y is logarithmic: equal distances are equal factors.

remember: ln tau = ln B + (E_eff / R)(1/T): a straight line in 1/T.
Hot is left. Short delay is bottom. A line from bottom left to top right is normal.
Slope in 1000/T units times 1000 R gives E_eff.
Always state p and phi: delay depends on both.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position on x encodes reciprocal temperature, position on y encodes the logarithm of the delay. Colour (and marker shape) separates equivalence ratios. Filled markers are measurements, solid lines are the model: two kinds of mark for two kinds of evidence, so they can be compared directly.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Delay changes by orders of magnitude with temperature, so a linear axis would crush the cold end. 1/T is the variable in which the Boltzmann factor is linear. Together they make agreement a visual property: a line through the markers.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: A log axis hides large relative errors that look small: a model that is off by a factor of two looks like a modest vertical gap. Scatter that is a constant factor looks constant everywhere. Without error bars on the markers, a reader cannot tell a fit from a coincidence.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A residual plot of ln(model / experiment) against 1000/T shows the same comparison without the compression. A parity plot of model against experiment collapses temperature entirely. Use the F9.1 form to show the trend and a residual panel to show the error.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add a second x axis along the top labelled in kelvin, a shaded band for the experimental uncertainty, and a small residual strip below sharing the x axis.

worked.title: Reading an apparent activation energy off the reference figure
worked.problem: The middle line (phi = 1) runs from about 1.5e-5 s at 1000/T = 0.8 to about 1.8e-3 s at 1000/T = 1.4. Estimate E_eff.
worked.answer: About 66 kJ/mol for these demonstration data, read by eye: good to perhaps 10 percent.

analyze.q: Which of the three series is the most sensitive to temperature? How do you know without reading numbers?
The markers at the cold end sit above the line for phi = 0.5 and phi = 1.0. What would you check first, and what would you change in the figure to make the question answerable?
analyze.hint: Measurement uncertainty grows at long delays; add error bars.

analyze.q: What would the same data look like against T instead of 1000/T?

evaluate.q: Is a plot with only three series and no error bars enough to claim that a mechanism is validated?
evaluate.hint: What range of pressure and composition does it cover?

checks.q: Why is hot on the left of this plot?
checks.answer: Because the x variable is reciprocal temperature: high T means small 1/T, so it sits at the left.

checks.q: Two points on a line are at 1000/T = 1.0 and 1.2 with delays 1e-4 s and 1e-3 s. What is E_eff?
The data are on a line at hot temperatures and flatten at cold ones. What does that say?
checks.hint: Slope falls toward the cold end.
checks.answer: The apparent activation energy falls with decreasing temperature: the controlling chemistry has changed. A single straight model line cannot capture that.
